title: Why Yagyas Don’t Bring Rain | Science Explains

description:
Can marrying frogs really bring rain? In India, bizarre rituals like frog weddings and Yagyas are still conducted with the belief that they can influence the weather. Politicians, priests, and villagers come together to perform these spectacles — from dipping MLAs in mud baths to chanting mantras around sacrificial fires — all in the name of rain. But does any of this actually work?

This video exposes the pseudoscience behind rainmaking rituals. We explain why asking “why does it rain after a Yagya?” is a loaded question — it assumes a false cause. Rain follows natural processes, not rituals. Water droplets condense in clouds, grow heavy, and fall as rain. Simple school-level science. Superstitions twist correlation into causation, convincing people that rituals cause rain just because they sometimes coincide with monsoon showers

We look at examples across history: costly Yagyas funded by governments, frog marriages from Gorakhpur to Assam, and even divorces of frogs after too much rain! Globally too, cultures tried rainmaking — from Native American rain dances to Chinese shamans and even a 1915 chemical “rainmaker” in California. These traditions reveal more about human psychology than meteorology.

The video also explores logical fallacies and cognitive biases:

Post hoc fallacy — assuming rain after ritual means ritual caused rain.
Confirmation bias — remembering the rare hits, ignoring the frequent misses.
Correlation vs causation — pattern-seeking brains finding links where none exist.

And as for the frogs, dressed up, paraded, and circled around fires — they’re just unwilling victims of human superstition. The truth is, if you want rain, try cloud seeding with silver iodide, not chanting mantras.

If you’ve searched for frog marriage India, Yagya rainmaking, pseudoscience rituals, post hoc fallacy explained, or superstition in India, this video gives you the rational perspective.

Don’t forget to like, comment, share, and hype this video to promote scientific temper over superstition.
